style: Comprehensive meaningful blend (interpretive text) + amplified study form; bare-transliteration in amp with Strong's carried in notes (matching the ch.1 pilot); em-dashes used sparingly.
chapterNote: Chapter 12 is a dense string of antithetical couplets that sort the whole of life into two columns: the righteous and the wicked, the diligent and the slack, the truthful tongue and the lying one. Its governing theme is rootedness and stability -- the righteous are a root that cannot be moved (vv. 3, 12), a house that stands (v. 7), while wickedness has no anchor and topples. A second strand runs through it: the deadly or healing power of speech (vv. 6, 13-14, 17-19, 22-23, 25), the wise mastery of the tongue. The chapter closes where Proverbs always points -- the road of righteousness is the road of life, with no death at its end (v. 28).

1.text: Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge, but the man who hates correction is no better than a brute beast.
1.amp: Whoever loves [ahab -- desires, delights in] discipline [musar -- corrective instruction, the formative kind that stings] loves knowledge [daat], but he who hates [sane -- is hostile to] reproof [tokachat -- rebuke, the searching word] is brutish [baar -- senseless as cattle, dull as a burning stump].
1.notes: musar (H4148) is the same painful-but-loving correction prized in 1:2-3; the test of a man's love for knowledge is whether he can stomach being corrected. baar (H1198) likens the reproof-hater to an animal -- all appetite, no understanding (cf. Ps 73:22).

2.text: A good man draws favor from the LORD, but the man full of schemes He pronounces guilty.
2.amp: A good [tov] man obtains favor [ratzon -- delight, acceptance, the gracious goodwill] of the LORD [YHWH], but a man [ish] of wicked devices [mezimmah -- scheming, calculated plotting] He will condemn [rasha -- declare guilty, sentence as a criminal].
2.notes: ratzon (H7522) is the favorable acceptance God shows toward the good man, the same word for the offering He delights to receive. mezimmah (H4209) is the 'gray' word for planning -- good as foresight in 2:11, here bent into scheming; the verb rasha (H7561) means to treat as wicked, to hand down a guilty verdict.

3.text: No one is made secure by wickedness, but the root of the righteous can never be uprooted.
3.amp: A man [adam] shall not be established [kun -- set firm, made to stand] by wickedness [resha], but the root [shoresh] of the righteous [tsaddiq] shall not be moved [mot -- totter, slip, be made to fall].
3.notes: kun (H3559) is to be fixed, firmly founded -- wickedness can never supply such a footing. The root-image recurs in v.12 and v.7's standing house: the tsaddiq (H6662) draws life from a hidden, immovable source, so he does not totter (mot, H4131) when the storm comes (cf. Ps 1:3; 15:5).

4.text: A wife of strong character is a crown to her husband, but the one who brings shame is like rot in his bones.
4.amp: A woman [ishshah] of valor [chayil -- strength, worth, the same word used of a mighty army] is a crown [atarah -- a regal wreath] to her husband [baal -- her lord and master], but she who makes ashamed [bosh] is as rottenness [raqab -- decay] in his bones [etsem].
4.notes: chayil (H2428) is military-grade strength and worth -- the 'virtuous' woman of 31:10 is the eshet-chayil, a woman of force and competence, not mere mildness. The contrast is brutal: a noble wife lifts a man like a crown (atarah, H5850); a disgraceful one is a slow decay (raqab, H7538) eating the very frame (etsem, H6106) that should support him.

5.text: The plans of the righteous are just, but the steering counsels of the wicked are nothing but treachery.
5.amp: The thoughts [machashabah -- plans, designs] of the righteous [tsaddiq] are right [mishpat -- just, conformed to right judgment], but the counsels [tachbulot -- the steering-strategies, the rope-handlings that turn a ship] of the wicked [rasha] are deceit [mirmah -- treachery, fraud].
5.notes: machashabah (H4284) is the inner plan; even the private reasoning of the righteous runs to mishpat (H4941), justice. tachbulot (H8458) is the same nautical word for steering wisely (1:5), but in the wicked the skillful steering serves mirmah (H4820) -- competence in the service of fraud.

6.text: The words of the wicked are an ambush for blood, but the speech of the upright rescues men from it.
6.amp: The words [dabar] of the wicked [rasha] are to lie in wait [arab -- ambush, crouch in hiding] for blood [dam], but the mouth [peh] of the upright [yashar] shall deliver [natsal -- snatch away, rescue] them.
6.notes: arab (H693) is the ambush-verb of 1:11, where the gang crouched for blood -- here it lives in their very speech. The same chapter that warns the tongue can kill (v.18) shows it can also save: the upright man's mouth becomes the natsal (H5337), the rescue that snatches the intended victims out of the trap.

7.text: The wicked are overthrown and gone, but the house of the righteous goes on standing.
7.amp: The wicked [rasha] are overthrown [haphak -- turned over, capsized], and are not, but the house [bayith] of the righteous [tsaddiq] shall stand [amad -- stand firm, remain, endure].
7.notes: haphak (H2015) is to overturn -- the verb for Sodom's destruction (Gen 19:25); the wicked are not merely defeated but tipped over and erased ('are not'). amad (H5975) is to keep standing, to endure -- the righteous house outlasts the catastrophe that capsizes the wicked (cf. Matt 7:24-27).

8.text: A man is praised in proportion to his good sense, but the twisted-minded earns only contempt.
8.amp: A man [ish] shall be commended [halal -- praised, made to shine] according to his wisdom [sekel -- good sense, prudence, sound insight], but he that is of a perverse [avah -- bent, crooked] heart shall be despised [buz -- held in contempt, scorned].
8.notes: sekel (H7922) is practical good sense, the insight that produces sound judgment -- and it, not wealth or birth, draws genuine praise (halal, H1984). The opposite is the man whose mind is bent out of true (avah, H5753), and a warped mind earns buz (H937), open contempt.

9.text: Better to be a man of no account who has a servant than to play the great one and go hungry.
9.amp: He that is despised [qalah -- lightly esteemed, thought little of], and has a servant [ebed], is better [tov] than he that honors [kabad -- makes himself heavy, glorifies himself] himself, and lacks bread [lechem].
9.notes: qalah (H7034) is to be held cheap, of low reputation; kabad (H3513) is literally to make oneself 'weighty,' to puff up one's own importance. Proverbs prefers modest substance to hollow display: a lowly man who can keep a servant outranks the self-important man with an empty table.

10.text: The righteous man cares even for the life of his animal, but the kindest feelings of the wicked are cruelty itself.
10.amp: A righteous [tsaddiq] man regards [yada -- knows, attends to, cares for] the life [nephesh -- the breath and being] of his beast [behemah], but the tender mercies [rachamim -- compassions, the womb-deep mercies] of the wicked [rasha] are cruel [akzari -- merciless, pitiless].
10.notes: yada (H3045), 'to know,' here means to know with care -- the righteous man's mercy reaches down even to his livestock (cf. Deut 25:4; Matt 12:11). The sting is the contrast: rachamim (H7356) are the deepest tendernesses a person has, and in the wicked even these are akzari (H394), cruel -- their very mercy wounds.

11.text: He who works his land will have bread to spare, but whoever chases empty fantasies has no sense at all.
11.amp: He that tills [abad -- serves, labors over] his land [adamah -- the ground, the soil] shall be satisfied [sabah -- filled to the full] with bread [lechem], but he that pursues [radaph -- chases, hunts after] vain [req -- empty, worthless] persons is void of understanding.
11.notes: abad (H5647) is the same verb for serving and worshiping -- honest labor of the soil is dignified, patient work. radaph (H7291), to chase, sets the diligent farmer against the dreamer who hunts after req (H7386), empty things; the WEB's 'fantasies' captures it -- to chase the worthless is to lack heart (leb), the seat of sense.

12.text: The wicked craves the spoils that evil men seize, but the root of the righteous bears its own fruit.
12.amp: The wicked [rasha] desires [chamad -- covets, longs for] the net [matsod -- the spoil, the plunder taken in the snare] of evil [ra] men, but the root [shoresh] of the righteous [tsaddiq] yields [natan -- gives, brings forth] fruit.
12.notes: chamad (H2530) is the covet-verb of the tenth commandment -- the wicked hungers for plunder he has not earned. The antithesis returns to v.3's root-image: the wicked grasps at another's net of spoil, but the tsaddiq needs no spoil, for his own root gives (natan, H5414) fruit from within (cf. Jer 17:8).

13.text: In the sin of his own lips the evil man is trapped, but the righteous escapes out of trouble.
13.amp: The wicked [ra] is snared [moqesh -- caught in a trap, taken by his own bait] by the transgression [pesha -- rebellion, willful sin] of his lips [saphah], but the just [tsaddiq] shall come out [yatsa -- go forth, emerge] of trouble [tsarah -- distress, the tight place].
13.notes: moqesh (H4170) is a fowler's trap -- the wicked man's own rebellious speech (pesha, H6588) becomes the snare that catches him (cf. v.6; Ps 7:15). The righteous, by contrast, simply walks out (yatsa, H3318) of tsarah (H6869), the pressing distress, free where the other is bound.

14.text: A man is filled with good by the fruit of his words, and the work of his hands comes back to him in kind.
14.amp: A man [ish] shall be satisfied [sabah -- filled full] with good [tov] by the fruit [peri] of his mouth [peh], and the recompense [gemul -- the dealing repaid, the just return] of a man's [adam] hands [yad] shall be rendered [shub -- returned, brought back] unto him.
14.notes: the fruit-of-the-mouth (peri-peh) echoes v.13 -- words bear harvest, for good or ill. gemul (H1576) is the deserved return, and shub (H7725), to come back around, is the law of moral reciprocity: what a man's hands do returns to his own door (cf. Gal 6:7).

15.text: The way of a fool looks right in his own eyes, but the wise man is the one who listens to counsel.
15.amp: The way [derek] of a fool [evil -- the morally dense, the willful fool] is right [yashar -- straight, upright] in his own eyes [ayin], but he that hearkens [shama -- hears and heeds] unto counsel [etsah -- advice, wise direction] is wise [chakam].
15.notes: the fool's fatal flaw is self-certainty -- his road seems yashar (H3477), straight, only because his own eye is the sole judge of it (cf. v.1; 3:7). The mark of the chakam (H2450) is the opposite reflex: he listens (shama, H8085), submitting his judgment to counsel rather than trusting himself alone.

16.text: A fool lets his anger blaze out the same day, but the prudent man passes over an insult and keeps it quiet.
16.amp: A fool's [evil] wrath [kaas -- vexation, hot provocation] is presently [bayom -- in that very day, at once] known [yada -- made known, shown plainly], but a prudent [arum -- shrewd, sensible] man covers [kasah -- conceals, passes over] shame [qalon -- insult, disgrace].
16.notes: the fool has no delay between offense and outburst -- his kaas (H3708) flares 'in that day' (bayom). arum (H6175) is shrewdness, the serpent's craftiness of 1:4 here turned to self-mastery: the prudent man kasah (H3680), covers over, an insult rather than broadcasting his wounded pride (cf. 10:12; 19:11).

17.text: The man who breathes out truth declares what is right, but a false witness breathes out deceit.
17.amp: He that speaks [puach -- breathes out, utters] truth [emunah -- faithfulness, reliability] shows forth [nagad -- declares, makes plain] righteousness [tsedek], but a false [sheqer -- lying] witness [ed] deceit [mirmah].
17.notes: emunah (H530) is more than accuracy -- it is faithful reliability, a character that can be leaned on; what such a man breathes out (puach, H6315) is tsedek (H6664), righteousness itself made public. The lying witness (ed sheqer) is the courtroom counterfeit, exhaling mirmah (H4820), fraud, where the other exhaled truth (cf. the ninth commandment).

18.text: There is a kind of reckless talk that stabs like a sword, but the tongue of the wise brings healing.
18.amp: There is one that speaks rashly [bata -- babbles, blurts out hastily] like the piercings of a sword [chereb], but the tongue [lashon] of the wise [chakam] is health [marpe -- healing, a cure].
18.notes: bata (H981) is to blurt without thought -- such careless words stab like a chereb (H2719), a sword, leaving wounds the speaker never weighed. The wise tongue is the antidote: lashon (H3956) under wisdom's rule becomes marpe (H4832), a healing medicine -- the same organ that kills can mend (cf. v.6; 15:4).

19.text: Truthful lips endure forever, but a lying tongue lasts only a moment.
19.amp: The lip [saphah] of truth [emeth -- truth, that which holds steady] shall be established [kun -- made firm, set to stand] forever [ad -- perpetuity], but a lying [sheqer] tongue [lashon] is but for a moment [raga -- the blink of an instant].
19.notes: emeth (H571) is truth as that which is firm and stands the test; truthful speech is kun (H3559), established, and lasts ad (H5703), into perpetuity. The lie has the lifespan of a raga (H7280) -- a single instant -- before it is exposed and gone; only truth has a future (cf. 1 Pet 1:25).

20.text: Deceit fills the hearts of those who plot evil, but joy belongs to those who counsel peace.
20.amp: Deceit [mirmah -- treachery, fraud] is in the heart [leb] of them that devise [charash -- plot in silence, forge as on an anvil] evil [ra], but to the counselors [yaats -- advisers] of peace [shalom -- wholeness, well-being] is joy [simchah].
20.notes: charash (H2790) means to engrave or forge silently -- the evil-plotter works in quiet, his leb full of mirmah (H4820). Against him stand the counselors of shalom (H7965), wholeness and peace, whose work yields simchah (H8057), gladness; they reap the joy they sow (cf. Matt 5:9).

21.text: No real harm overtakes the righteous, but the wicked are filled to the brim with trouble.
21.amp: There shall no evil [aven -- iniquity, calamity, harm] happen [anah -- befall, meet by appointment] to the just [tsaddiq], but the wicked [rasha] shall be filled [male -- be made full] with mischief [ra -- evil, trouble].
21.notes: aven (H205) carries both the sin and its sorrow; the righteous is not promised a painless life but a kept life -- no ultimate harm anah (H579), befalls him by God's appointment (cf. Rom 8:28). The wicked, by contrast, are male (H4390), filled up, with the very ra (H7451) they sought to deal others.

22.text: Lying lips are detestable to the LORD, but those who deal faithfully are His delight.
22.amp: Lying [sheqer] lips [saphah] are abomination [toebah -- a detestable thing, loathsome to God] to the LORD [YHWH], but they that deal [asah -- do, practice] truly [emunah -- in faithfulness] are His delight [ratzon -- pleasure, gracious acceptance].
22.notes: toebah (H8441) is the strongest word of divine revulsion, used of idolatry and injustice -- lying lips rank among the things God loathes (cf. 6:16-19). The opposite of mere truthful speech is to do (asah, H6213) faithfulness, to live emunah out in conduct; such people are His ratzon (H7522), the very delight He receives like a pleasing offering (cf. v.2).

23.text: A prudent man keeps his knowledge to himself, but the heart of fools blurts out their folly.
23.amp: A prudent [arum -- shrewd, discreet] man conceals [kasah -- covers, holds back] knowledge [daat], but the heart [leb] of fools [kesil -- the dull, thick-headed fool] proclaims [qara -- cries out, publishes aloud] foolishness [ivvelet -- folly].
23.notes: the arum (H6175) of v.16 returns -- discretion knows when to hold knowledge back rather than parade it (cf. 10:14). The kesil (H3684), the dull fool, has no such restraint: his very heart qara (H7121), calls out, broadcasting his ivvelet (H200) for all to hear -- folly cannot keep silent.

24.text: The hand of the diligent will rule, but laziness ends in forced labor.
24.amp: The hand [yad] of the diligent [charuts -- sharp, eager, hard-working] shall bear rule [mashal -- govern, have dominion], but the slothful [remiyah -- slackness, also deceit] shall be put to forced labor [mas -- tribute, the corvée of conscripted toil].
24.notes: charuts (H2742) pictures the sharp, decisive worker whose diligence lifts him to mashal (H4910), dominion -- diligence rises, slackness sinks. remiyah (H7423) is slackness that shades into deceit; its end is mas (H4522), the forced labor-gang -- the lazy man ends up serving where the diligent man rules (cf. v.27; 10:4).

25.text: Anxiety in a man's heart weighs it down, but a good word lifts it up with gladness.
25.amp: Heaviness [deagah -- anxious dread, gnawing care] in the heart [leb] of man [ish] makes it stoop [shachah -- bow down, sink low], but a good [tov] word [dabar] makes it glad [samach -- rejoices, brightens].
25.notes: deagah (H1674) is the anxious care that drags a man down; shachah (H7812), to bow low, is elsewhere the verb for worship -- here it is the heart bent under its burden. The remedy is small and within anyone's reach: a single tov dabar, a good word, can samach (H8055), gladden, the very heart that worry had bowed (cf. v.18; 15:23).

26.text: The righteous man guides his neighbor rightly, but the way of the wicked leads them astray.
26.amp: The righteous [tsaddiq] is a guide [tur -- searches out and shows the way] to his neighbor [rea -- friend, companion], but the way [derek] of the wicked [rasha] seduces [taah -- leads astray, causes to wander] them.
26.notes: tur (H8446) is to scout out and explore -- the righteous man searches out the good road and shows his rea (H7453), his neighbor, the way (the textual sense behind 'more excellent than'). The wicked do the reverse: their very derek (H1870), their path, is a taah (H8582), a wandering-off that leads astray both themselves and those who follow.

27.text: The slothful man does not even roast the game he caught, but diligence is a man's most precious possession.
27.amp: The slothful [remiyah -- the slack, lazy one] roasts [charak -- sears, cooks] not that which he took in hunting [tsayid -- his game, the prey he caught], but the substance [hon -- wealth, riches] of a diligent [charuts -- eager, hard-working] man is precious [yaqar -- prized, rare, of great worth].
27.notes: charak (H2760) is to roast over fire -- the slothful man (remiyah, H7423) is so slack he will not even finish the meat his own hunt secured, letting the catch rot. Against such wasted labor, the diligent man's diligence is itself his hon (H1952), his wealth -- a thing yaqar (H3368), precious and rare (cf. v.24).

28.text: On the road of righteousness there is life, and along that pathway death does not lie.
28.amp: In the way [orach -- the path, the well-trodden road] of righteousness [tsedaqah] is life [chay -- living, the fullness of life], and in the pathway [netivah -- the trodden trail] thereof there is no death [maveth].
28.notes: orach (H734) and netivah (H5410) are both worn-in tracks -- the way of tsedaqah (H6666) is no untried theory but a road already walked. Its end is chay (H2416), life, and emphatically 'no death' (maveth, H4194): the chapter that began with two columns ends with two destinies, and the righteous road runs clear through death into life (cf. 4:18; John 8:51).
